Write helpful notes in free-form prose, with optional headings or lists.
There is no required schema, JSON object or special block.
Include short supporting quotes and relevant context where useful.
Separate explicit supporting facts, explicit contradictions and mere mentions.
Do not add outside knowledge or invent missing facts to complete an answer.

dates or conditions into source claims unless page_text independently states them.

enough; do not construct a complete answer or a table of satisfied conditions

Source: https://www.airtraveler.club/insider/safety-record/eight-fatal-business-jet-accidents-2024-and-no-way-to-verify-operator-safety/
Title: Eight fatal business-jet accidents in 2024 — and no way to verify operator safety
Chunks: 5,6,7,8
## Why the SMS rule is a forward-looking variable, not a proven fix
The FAA’s Part 5 Safety Management Systems rule took effect on **May 28, 2024**. It requires Part 135 charter operators to build a formal SMS — a structured way of identifying and managing operational risk before it turns into an accident.
Compliance unfolds in phases rather than all at once. For operators already holding a Part 135 certificate, the deadline to build and roll out an SMS and file a declaration of compliance is generally **May 28, 2027**. Anyone applying for a new Part 135 certificate on or after May 28, 2024 must have an SMS in place during certification.
There’s a wrinkle worth knowing: the mandate isn’t confined to Part 135. Part 91 operators holding a qualifying §91.147 letter of authorization — typically air-tour or certain commercial sightseeing operations — are also subject to the SMS requirement by the same 2027 deadline.
What the rule has not yet produced is measurable safety gain. The mandate is recent enough that outcome data does not exist, and the reviewed evidence shows no verified split by operator size. Treat it as a variable to watch, not a trend already in motion.

## What this means for you
Start by getting the legal operating carrier and the assigned aircraft registration from the broker, then confirm both against the FAA’s Part 135 list. That list refreshes each week and can be searched by operator name, doing-business-as name, or aircraft registration. What it establishes is legal charter authority — not a comparative safety score.
Next, ask which _ARGUS_, _Wyvern_, or IS-BAO designation the operator currently holds, at what tier, along with the date of its most recent audit. Ask for the operator’s name, not just the broker’s.
Each program evaluates a different dimension — IS-BAO gauges how mature an operator’s safety-management system is, while ARGUS and Wyvern apply their own evaluation frameworks.
Then ask the question the “private jet” label quietly dodges: will this flight operate under Part 135 or under private Part 91 authority? A bare “safety rated” claim with no named program, no level, no audit date, and no match to the operating carrier should be treated as insufficient. A review by Bravo found no shared industry-wide scale and no single authoritative public database behind these ratings.
One more check worth doing: verifying a single tail number is narrower than assessing the operator as a whole. The aircraft assigned to your trip may be one of many the operator flies. When the trip is over, store the certificate and rating documents with the booking record.
Reporting by
ATC Intelligence
ATC Intelligence is the research division of Air Traveler Club. Backed by 15 years in Asia-Pacific aviation, we don't just report on the regional market; we live and work in it. By pairing AI-driven data with strict human fact-checking, we provide actionable, trustworthy journalism designed to make your trips to Asia smarter and more affordable.
Follow our daily coverage on Google News, Google Discover, and social media.

## Key terms
Part 91 Part 91 is the FAA rule set covering private and corporate flying, including aircraft flown by their owners. Flights under Part 91 hold no certificate to carry paying passengers on demand, so they carry fewer of the training, maintenance, and oversight obligations that apply to charter work. For a traveler, the practical consequence is that a “private” label says nothing about oversight — only the certificate behind the flight does.Part 135 Part 135 is the FAA category for on-demand charter and air-taxi operations flown for hire. Operators in this category must hold an FAA certificate and meet structured maintenance, pilot-training, and oversight requirements that private flying does not. Because Part 135 operators are the ones most travelers actually fly with when they book a charter, the certificate — not the aircraft — is the thing worth verifying before a trip.SMS (Safety Management Systems)A Safety Management System, or SMS, is a formal, documented process an operator uses to identify and manage operational risk before it becomes an accident. The FAA’s Part 5 rule, effective May 28, 2024, requires Part 135 charter operators to build one, with existing certificate holders generally given until May 28, 2027 to implement it and file a declaration of compliance. Because the mandate is still phasing in, an operator’s SMS status today says more about its paperwork timeline than about its measured safety record.IS-BAO IS-BAO, the International Standard for Business Aircraft Operations, is a voluntary audit program that measures how mature an operator’s safety-management system is. It sits outside FAA certification, and the reviewed evidence does not establish a common industry-wide scale or a single authoritative public database covering it alongside ARGUS and Wyvern. For a traveler, an IS-BAO designation is only meaningful when paired with the specific tier and the date of the most recent audit — a bare “rated” claim tells you little.FBO An FBO, or fixed-base operator, is the business that provides ground services such as fueling, hangaring, and passenger handling at an airport. Private and charter flights typically depart from an FBO rather than an airline terminal, which is why two very different operations can share the same lounge. In this article, the FBO is the setting where the Part 91 and Part 135 distinction becomes invisible — the ramp and the cabin look identical even when the rules behind them do not.

## Questions? Answers.
Can I check a private jet operator’s safety record before I book?  
You can verify legal charter authority, but not a comparative safety score. You can search the FAA’s Part 135 operator list — refreshed each week — by operator name, doing-business-as name, or aircraft registration; use it to confirm the legal carrier and aircraft before you book.
Is a Part 135 charter safer than an owner-flown Part 91 flight?  
Directionally, yes — Part 135 operations carry stricter oversight, training, and maintenance requirements than private Part 91 flying. But the exact gap is not verifiable from the reviewed material: no fatal accident rate per 100,000 flight hours exists for Part 91 business jets alone, and the requested Part 135 figures of 0.76 total and 0.201 fatal were not confirmed. The 2024 baseline is eight fatal business-jet accidents and 21 fatalities.
What do ARGUS, Wyvern, and IS-BAO ratings actually tell a traveler?  
They are voluntary programs that sit outside FAA certification, and each evaluates a different dimension of an operator’s safety posture. No shared industry-wide scale or single authoritative public database covers these ratings, so a “rated” claim without a named program, tier, and audit date tells you very little.
Has the 2024 Part 135 SMS rule already made charter flying safer?  
Not measurably — the rule is too recent for outcome data to exist. It took effect May 28, 2024, and existing certificate holders generally have until May 28, 2027 to implement an SMS and file a declaration of compliance. New applicants submitting on or after May 28, 2024 must have an SMS during certification.

## Why the SMS rule is a forward-looking variable, not a proven fix
The FAA’s Part 5 Safety Management Systems rule took effect on **May 28, 2024**. It requires Part 135 charter operators to build a formal SMS — a structured way of identifying and managing operational risk before it turns into an accident.
Compliance unfolds in phases rather than all at once. For operators already holding a Part 135 certificate, the deadline to build and roll out an SMS and file a declaration of compliance is generally **May 28, 2027**. Anyone applying for a new Part 135 certificate on or after May 28, 2024 must have an SMS in place during certification.
There’s a wrinkle worth knowing: the mandate isn’t confined to Part 135. Part 91 operators holding a qualifying §91.147 letter of authorization — typically air-tour or certain commercial sightseeing operations — are also subject to the SMS requirement by the same 2027 deadline.
What the rule has not yet produced is measurable safety gain. The mandate is recent enough that outcome data does not exist, and the reviewed evidence shows no verified split by operator size. Treat it as a variable to watch, not a trend already in motion.
texts.6:
## What this means for you
Start by getting the legal operating carrier and the assigned aircraft registration from the broker, then confirm both against the FAA’s Part 135 list. That list refreshes each week and can be searched by operator name, doing-business-as name, or aircraft registration. What it establishes is legal charter authority — not a comparative safety score.
Next, ask which _ARGUS_, _Wyvern_, or IS-BAO designation the operator currently holds, at what tier, along with the date of its most recent audit. Ask for the operator’s name, not just the broker’s.
Each program evaluates a different dimension — IS-BAO gauges how mature an operator’s safety-management system is, while ARGUS and Wyvern apply their own evaluation frameworks.
Then ask the question the “private jet” label quietly dodges: will this flight operate under Part 135 or under private Part 91 authority? A bare “safety rated” claim with no named program, no level, no audit date, and no match to the operating carrier should be treated as insufficient. A review by Bravo found no shared industry-wide scale and no single authoritative public database behind these ratings.
One more check worth doing: verifying a single tail number is narrower than assessing the operator as a whole. The aircraft assigned to your trip may be one of many the operator flies. When the trip is over, store the certificate and rating documents with the booking record.

## Key terms
Part 91 Part 91 is the FAA rule set covering private and corporate flying, including aircraft flown by their owners. Flights under Part 91 hold no certificate to carry paying passengers on demand, so they carry fewer of the training, maintenance, and oversight obligations that apply to charter work. For a traveler, the practical consequence is that a “private” label says nothing about oversight — only the certificate behind the flight does.Part 135 Part 135 is the FAA category for on-demand charter and air-taxi operations flown for hire. Operators in this category must hold an FAA certificate and meet structured maintenance, pilot-training, and oversight requirements that private flying does not. Because Part 135 operators are the ones most travelers actually fly with when they book a charter, the certificate — not the aircraft — is the thing worth verifying before a trip.SMS (Safety Management Systems)A Safety Management System, or SMS, is a formal, documented process an operator uses to identify and manage operational risk before it becomes an accident. The FAA’s Part 5 rule, effective May 28, 2024, requires Part 135 charter operators to build one, with existing certificate holders generally given until May 28, 2027 to implement it and file a declaration of compliance. Because the mandate is still phasing in, an operator’s SMS status today says more about its paperwork timeline than about its measured safety record.IS-BAO IS-BAO, the International Standard for Business Aircraft Operations, is a voluntary audit program that measures how mature an operator’s safety-management system is. It sits outside FAA certification, and the reviewed evidence does not establish a common industry-wide scale or a single authoritative public database covering it alongside ARGUS and Wyvern. For a traveler, an IS-BAO designation is only meaningful when paired with the specific tier and the date of the most recent audit — a bare “rated” claim tells you little.FBO An FBO, or fixed-base operator, is the business that provides ground services such as fueling, hangaring, and passenger handling at an airport. Private and charter flights typically depart from an FBO rather than an airline terminal, which is why two very different operations can share the same lounge. In this article, the FBO is the setting where the Part 91 and Part 135 distinction becomes invisible — the ramp and the cabin look identical even when the rules behind them do not.
texts.8:
## Questions? Answers.
Can I check a private jet operator’s safety record before I book?  
You can verify legal charter authority, but not a comparative safety score. You can search the FAA’s Part 135 operator list — refreshed each week — by operator name, doing-business-as name, or aircraft registration; use it to confirm the legal carrier and aircraft before you book.
Is a Part 135 charter safer than an owner-flown Part 91 flight?  
Directionally, yes — Part 135 operations carry stricter oversight, training, and maintenance requirements than private Part 91 flying. But the exact gap is not verifiable from the reviewed material: no fatal accident rate per 100,000 flight hours exists for Part 91 business jets alone, and the requested Part 135 figures of 0.76 total and 0.201 fatal were not confirmed. The 2024 baseline is eight fatal business-jet accidents and 21 fatalities.
What do ARGUS, Wyvern, and IS-BAO ratings actually tell a traveler?  
They are voluntary programs that sit outside FAA certification, and each evaluates a different dimension of an operator’s safety posture. No shared industry-wide scale or single authoritative public database covers these ratings, so a “rated” claim without a named program, tier, and audit date tells you very little.
Has the 2024 Part 135 SMS rule already made charter flying safer?  
Not measurably — the rule is too recent for outcome data to exist. It took effect May 28, 2024, and existing certificate holders generally have until May 28, 2027 to implement an SMS and file a declaration of compliance. New applicants submitting on or after May 28, 2024 must have an SMS during certification.

Next, ask which _ARGUS_, _Wyvern_, or IS-BAO designation the operator currently holds, at what tier, along with the date of its most recent audit. Ask for the operator’s name, not just the broker’s.
Each program evaluates a different dimension — IS-BAO gauges how mature an operator’s safety-management system is, while ARGUS and Wyvern apply their own evaluation frameworks.
Then ask the question the “private jet” label quietly dodges: will this flight operate under Part 135 or under private Part 91 authority? A bare “safety rated” claim with no named program, no level, no audit date, and no match to the operating carrier should be treated as insufficient. A review by Bravo found no shared industry-wide scale and no single authoritative public database behind these ratings.
One more check worth doing: verifying a single tail number is narrower than assessing the operator as a whole. The aircraft assigned to your trip may be one of many the operator flies. When the trip is over, store the certificate and rating documents with the booking record.
Reporting by
ATC Intelligence
ATC Intelligence is the research division of Air Traveler Club. Backed by 15 years in Asia-Pacific aviation, we don't just report on the regional market; we live and work in it. By pairing AI-driven data with strict human fact-checking, we provide actionable, trustworthy journalism designed to make your trips to Asia smarter and more affordable.
Follow our daily coverage on Google News, Google Discover, and social media.

## Key terms
Part 91 Part 91 is the FAA rule set covering private and corporate flying, including aircraft flown by their owners. Flights under Part 91 hold no certificate to carry paying passengers on demand, so they carry fewer of the training, maintenance, and oversight obligations that apply to charter work. For a traveler, the practical consequence is that a “private” label says nothing about oversight — only the certificate behind the flight does.Part 135 Part 135 is the FAA category for on-demand charter and air-taxi operations flown for hire. Operators in this category must hold an FAA certificate and meet structured maintenance, pilot-training, and oversight requirements that private flying does not. Because Part 135 operators are the ones most travelers actually fly with when they book a charter, the certificate — not the aircraft — is the thing worth verifying before a trip.SMS (Safety Management Systems)A Safety Management System, or SMS, is a formal, documented process an operator uses to identify and manage operational risk before it becomes an accident. The FAA’s Part 5 rule, effective May 28, 2024, requires Part 135 charter operators to build one, with existing certificate holders generally given until May 28, 2027 to implement it and file a declaration of compliance. Because the mandate is still phasing in, an operator’s SMS status today says more about its paperwork timeline than about its measured safety record.IS-BAO IS-BAO, the International Standard for Business Aircraft Operations, is a voluntary audit program that measures how mature an operator’s safety-management system is. It sits outside FAA certification, and the reviewed evidence does not establish a common industry-wide scale or a single authoritative public database covering it alongside ARGUS and Wyvern. For a traveler, an IS-BAO designation is only meaningful when paired with the specific tier and the date of the most recent audit — a bare “rated” claim tells you little.FBO An FBO, or fixed-base operator, is the business that provides ground services such as fueling, hangaring, and passenger handling at an airport. Private and charter flights typically depart from an FBO rather than an airline terminal, which is why two very different operations can share the same lounge. In this article, the FBO is the setting where the Part 91 and Part 135 distinction becomes invisible — the ramp and the cabin look identical even when the rules behind them do not.

## Questions? Answers.
Can I check a private jet operator’s safety record before I book?  
You can verify legal charter authority, but not a comparative safety score. You can search the FAA’s Part 135 operator list — refreshed each week — by operator name, doing-business-as name, or aircraft registration; use it to confirm the legal carrier and aircraft before you book.
Is a Part 135 charter safer than an owner-flown Part 91 flight?  
Directionally, yes — Part 135 operations carry stricter oversight, training, and maintenance requirements than private Part 91 flying. But the exact gap is not verifiable from the reviewed material: no fatal accident rate per 100,000 flight hours exists for Part 91 business jets alone, and the requested Part 135 figures of 0.76 total and 0.201 fatal were not confirmed. The 2024 baseline is eight fatal business-jet accidents and 21 fatalities.
What do ARGUS, Wyvern, and IS-BAO ratings actually tell a traveler?  
They are voluntary programs that sit outside FAA certification, and each evaluates a different dimension of an operator’s safety posture. No shared industry-wide scale or single authoritative public database covers these ratings, so a “rated” claim without a named program, tier, and audit date tells you very little.
Has the 2024 Part 135 SMS rule already made charter flying safer?  
Not measurably — the rule is too recent for outcome data to exist. It took effect May 28, 2024, and existing certificate holders generally have until May 28, 2027 to implement an SMS and file a declaration of compliance. New applicants submitting on or after May 28, 2024 must have an SMS during certification.

EDITOR’S NOTE: For the latest developments, follow our updated coverage here.
A private jet traveling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas careened into the ground in Palm Beach County, Florida, Sunday afternoon, leaving a deep crater and burning debris just feet from nearby homes and businesses and killing all nine on board, officials say.
Video from a passing vehicle shows the jet, a Learjet 60, slamming down nose first on a busy roadway in a flash before a fireball erupts.
“It was a cataclysmic plane crash,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said. “It looked like a missile going down.”
There were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured.
A large, fiery and smoky crater was left behind after a Learjet carrying nine people crashed in Palm Beach County, Florida
0:15  • Source: CNN
A large, fiery and smoky crater was left behind after a Learjet carrying nine people crashed in Palm Beach ...
0:15
Before the crash,the pilot calmly reported ice accumulating on the aircraft, with an outside air temperature of -47 degrees Celsius, and moderate turbulence, bouncing the plane by up to 700 feet, according to a recording of air traffic control radio calls captured by LiveATC.net.
But moments later, the pilot began to sound more panicked.
“Mayday, mayday,” the pilot told the Miami Air Route Traffic Control Center. “We’re descending 10,000 feet per minute!”
“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” they yelled, “We’re going to crash into the ground!”
Audio captures moments before Learjet crash
Minutes before the crash, the pilot of the plane reported ice accumulating on the aircraft, an outside air temperature of -47 degrees Celsius, and moderate turbulence.
Source: LiveATC.com
The jet descended 27,000 feet over the course of one minute, just before flight tracking data cut off, the website ADS-B Exchange shows.
Officials have not said what caused the jet to crash, and they have not identified the nine who died or said how many were passengers and crew.

There were scattered storms in the area at the time, and the plane passed through a stronger storm cell a few minutes before it began descending, but it is unclear if the storm contributed to the crash.
A news conference is expected Monday as authorities from the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board investigate.’

0:20  • Source: CNN
Rubble and smoke after a Learjet with 9 aboard crashed and erupted in Palm Beach, Florida, on Sunday
0:20

## ‘I heard and felt the boom’
The crash marks the second deadliest plane crash in the United States this year, according to NTSB records, after 12 people died in June when a skydiving plane crashed in Butler, Missouri. It is also the worst crash involving a Learjet 60, according to data from the Flight Safety Foundation. In 2008, four people were killed when a Learjet 60 bound for Los Angeles crashed on takeoff from Columbia, South Carolina.
The plane hit the ground shortly before 1 p.m. on Military Trail, a major thoroughfare between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North, the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office said.The roadway was left shattered and burning debris dotted the crater, video from CNN affiliate WPBF showed.
“There is a lot of debris that was strewn as a result of this crash,” DeSantis said.
The scene is just miles from the airport in West Palm Beach that was recently renamed for President Donald Trump and his Mar-A-Lago resort.
About 600 people are in need of shelter because the damage on the ground is blocking the entrance of a mobile home park, said Joel Flores, Palm Beach County commissioner for District 3, who was the first county official at the scene. Residents are being sent to two shelters in the county while the site is being investigated, he said.
“I heard and felt the boom,” Andrew Mannino told CNN. “The power immediately went out and is still out.”
Mannino said he smelled the smoke and “saw a large black cloud immerse in the air.”
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called the crash a “horrific tragedy.”
Dash cam video showing the crash is going to be important to investigators piecing together what happened, said Mary Schiavo, CNN aviation analyst and former inspector general for the Transportation Department.
“That is not a controlled descent,” Schiavo told CNN’s Fredricka Whitfield Sunday. “It’s clear, whatever happened, they had lost control of the plane.”
The steep descent could have forced parts of the plane to break off and the flight data recorder could have been destroyed in the explosion, she added.
Investigators will also have to piece together whether the environment played a part in the crash.

## ‘I heard and felt the boom’
Ice on wings and other surfaces can also pose a major threat to private jets. In January 2024, the NTSB published a safety alert underscoring the risks of in-flight icing conditions, which can cause pilots to lose control. The agency warned ice can “make managing the airplane’s flightpath and airspeed more difficult and can prevent the airplane from maintaining level flight.”

0:07  • Source: CNN
Smoke fills the sky after a Learjet with 9 aboard crashing and erupting into flames in Palm Beach ...
0:07
It’s not clear if the plane had a cockpit voice recorder on board, but FAA regulations require jet aircraft with more than one engine to carry a voice recorder if they are flown for hire.
The plane is registered to an LLC in Delaware, according to FAA records, and is listed as available for charter online.
_This story has been updated with additional information._
CNN meteorologist Tyler Ory and CNN’s Amanda Jackson and Nic Anderson contributed to this report.

EDITOR’S NOTE: For the latest developments, follow our updated coverage here.
A private jet traveling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas careened into the ground in Palm Beach County, Florida, Sunday afternoon, leaving a deep crater and burning debris just feet from nearby homes and businesses and killing all nine on board, officials say.
Video from a passing vehicle shows the jet, a Learjet 60, slamming down nose first on a busy roadway in a flash before a fireball erupts.
“It was a cataclysmic plane crash,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said. “It looked like a missile going down.”
There were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured.

Before the crash,the pilot calmly reported ice accumulating on the aircraft, with an outside air temperature of -47 degrees Celsius, and moderate turbulence, bouncing the plane by up to 700 feet, according to a recording of air traffic control radio calls captured by LiveATC.net.
But moments later, the pilot began to sound more panicked.
“Mayday, mayday,” the pilot told the Miami Air Route Traffic Control Center. “We’re descending 10,000 feet per minute!”
“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” they yelled, “We’re going to crash into the ground!”
Audio captures moments before Learjet crash
Minutes before the crash, the pilot of the plane reported ice accumulating on the aircraft, an outside air temperature of -47 degrees Celsius, and moderate turbulence.
Source: LiveATC.com
The jet descended 27,000 feet over the course of one minute, just before flight tracking data cut off, the website ADS-B Exchange shows.
Officials have not said what caused the jet to crash, and they have not identified the nine who died or said how many were passengers and crew.

There were scattered storms in the area at the time, and the plane passed through a stronger storm cell a few minutes before it began descending, but it is unclear if the storm contributed to the crash.

## ‘I heard and felt the boom’
The crash marks the second deadliest plane crash in the United States this year, according to NTSB records, after 12 people died in June when a skydiving plane crashed in Butler, Missouri. It is also the worst crash involving a Learjet 60, according to data from the Flight Safety Foundation. In 2008, four people were killed when a Learjet 60 bound for Los Angeles crashed on takeoff from Columbia, South Carolina.
The plane hit the ground shortly before 1 p.m. on Military Trail, a major thoroughfare between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North, the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office said.The roadway was left shattered and burning debris dotted the crater, video from CNN affiliate WPBF showed.
“There is a lot of debris that was strewn as a result of this crash,” DeSantis said.
The scene is just miles from the airport in West Palm Beach that was recently renamed for President Donald Trump and his Mar-A-Lago resort.
About 600 people are in need of shelter because the damage on the ground is blocking the entrance of a mobile home park, said Joel Flores, Palm Beach County commissioner for District 3, who was the first county official at the scene. Residents are being sent to two shelters in the county while the site is being investigated, he said.
“I heard and felt the boom,” Andrew Mannino told CNN. “The power immediately went out and is still out.”
Mannino said he smelled the smoke and “saw a large black cloud immerse in the air.”
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called the crash a “horrific tragedy.”
Dash cam video showing the crash is going to be important to investigators piecing together what happened, said Mary Schiavo, CNN aviation analyst and former inspector general for the Transportation Department.
“That is not a controlled descent,” Schiavo told CNN’s Fredricka Whitfield Sunday. “It’s clear, whatever happened, they had lost control of the plane.”
The steep descent could have forced parts of the plane to break off and the flight data recorder could have been destroyed in the explosion, she added.
Investigators will also have to piece together whether the environment played a part in the crash.

## ‘I heard and felt the boom’
Ice on wings and other surfaces can also pose a major threat to private jets. In January 2024, the NTSB published a safety alert underscoring the risks of in-flight icing conditions, which can cause pilots to lose control. The agency warned ice can “make managing the airplane’s flightpath and airspeed more difficult and can prevent the airplane from maintaining level flight.”

opened.information:
Source: https://abc7ny.com/story/35-military-jet-crashes-miramar-san-diego/19607645/
Title: Marine Corps says F-35B stealth fighter crashed near San Diego, pilot ejected
Chunks: 0,1,2
SAN DIEGO -- The U.S. Marine Corps says the pilot of an F-35B stealth fighter is expected to live after ejecting from the jet before it crashed in California.
The jet went down Friday near the Miramar air base in San Diego. “The pilot ejected, was transported to a local medical facility in stable condition for evaluation and treatment of non-life-threatening injuries,” the Marine Corps said in an updated statement.
Aerial video from a news helicopter showed a plume of black smoke rising from the wreckage in a dirt field, with multiple military and firefighting vehicles and people standing nearby. What appeared to be white flame retardant covered the ground, and at least one person was spraying the wreckage with a fire hose.
Wade Lott saw the crash as he drove to work at a concrete company just south of the flight line.
“It just blew up, it was crazy,” said Lott, 36, who watched from his truck as two jets descended toward the runway together. The first landed without incident, but the second suddenly began slowing down, almost as if it were trying to hover, Lott said. When the jet was about 100 feet (30 m) above the ground, the pilot ejected and their parachute deployed as they rose about 200 feet (61 m) into the air just in time.
“The jet hit the ground right next to another plane,” said Lott. “It plowed into the runway and just blew up.”
Candace Hadley, a spokesperson for San Diego Fire, said firefighters were on scene to respond to a vegetation fire that sparked near the crash site. She referred additional questions to Marine Corps Air Station Miramar.
The base used to host the Navy fighter pilot training school depicted in the original “Top Gun” movie, and was known as “Fightertown USA” in its heyday. The school was relocated to Naval Air Station Fallon in Nevada in 1996 after the base was transferred to the Marine Corps.

The U.S. Marine Corps, Navy and Air Force together have more than 630 F-35s, according to a 2024 analysis by the Government Accounting Office, which estimated the overall price tag to be $2 trillion at that point. The F-35B is one of several versions, and has an engine designed for short takeoffs and vertical landings. A single F-35B costs about $109 million.

## Top Stories
A Marines statement called Friday’s crash a “Class A mishap.” That’s the most severe mishap category, used when the damage totals more than $2 million, an aircraft is destroyed or a service member killed. In the Air Force alone, there have been at least 17 other “Class A mishaps” involving F-35 aircraft since 2000, according to Air Force Safety Center statistics.
At least seven other military aircraft mishaps have happened in the U.S. this year, according to the Flight Safety Foundation’s Aviation Safety Network database.
The F-35s are considered the safest and most capable fighter jets the military has in its fleet, according to the Lexington Institute think tank that focuses on defense technology and national security.
There have been fewer crashes involving any of the F-35 models since the jet was adopted in 2015 compared to other fighters when those planes were new, and fatal crashes are rare in F-35s.
In five F-35 crashes, the pilots were able to eject, though at least one sustained injuries. That pilot was injured when an F-35 crashed near the international airport in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in May 2024. The jet was heading an Air Force base in California from Texas.
___
_AP Transportation Writer Josh Funk contributed to this report from Omaha, Nebraska. Rebecca Boone contributed from Boise, Idaho._

Chunks: 0,1,2,3
Date:Sunday 12 May 2024

Piper PA-46-500TP Malibu Meridian  
Owner/operator:Bryants Aviation Inc  
Registration:N241PM  
MSN:4697150  
Year of manufacture:2003  
Fatalities:Fatalities: 2 / Occupants: 2  
Other fatalities:0  
Aircraft damage:Destroyed  
Category:Accident  
Location:near Marianna, AR - United States of America  
Phase:En route  
Nature:Private  
Departure airport:Pensacola Regional Airport, FL (PNS/KPNS)  
Destination airport:Batesville Regional Airport, AR (BVX/KBVX)  
Investigating agency:NTSB  
Confidence Rating: Accident investigation report completed and information captured
Narrative:
On May 12, 2024, about 1956 central daylight time, a Piper PA46-500TP airplane, N241PM, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Marianna, Arkansas. The pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.   
The pilot departed about 1721 central daylight time (all times CDT unless otherwise noted) on an instrument flight rules cross-country flight with one passenger and two dogs. After departure, the airplane turned onto a northwesterly track toward the destination. The pilot requested flight level (FL) 280 and, at 1841, reported to air traffic control (ATC) that his satellite weather radar was not functioning; he later asked for assistance navigating through weather. At 1908, he reported light chop over the previous 40 miles but that the flight was currently smooth.

At 1944, ATC instructed the pilot to descend to FL 240 and the pilot then checked in with a new ATC center on his route and reported descending with moderate chop. ATC responded by instructing the pilot to descend at his discretion to 17,000 ft msl (all altitudes in msl unless otherwise noted). The airplane reached FL 240 (the previously instructed altitude) at 1949, where it stayed for less than a minute before continuing its descent. The first portion of this descent was at a rate of 2,000 ft/min before slowing to about 1,000 ft/min.
At 1954, while the airplane was descending through 20,000 ft, ATC instructed the pilot to descend at his discretion to 6,000 ft. The airplane's rate of descent increased to more than 3,000 ft/min, and the airspeed markedly increased from 170 kts to over 200 kts, exceeding the airplane's maximum operation limit of 187 kts calibrated airspeed; the airplane was at risk of structural damage when exceeding this limitation.
Data showed that the airplane's descent then arrested about 18,000 ft (which ADS-B data recorded as the selected altitude) and it began a small climb as the airplane's airspeed began to slow below 170 kts. At the same time, the airplane began a slight right turn off of its original course that was consistent with the airplane no longer under autopilot control. Twenty seconds later, the airplane began to rapidly descend in a tightening right turn while the calibrated airspeed rapidly increased, again surpassing the maximum operation limit. ATC simultaneously lost communication and radar contact with the airplane at 7,800 ft msl. The controller attempted to contact the pilot with no response. ATC then issued an alert notification (ALNOT) and a search began.

Weather radar imagery showed the airplane encountering light intensity echoes as it descended from 24,000 ft consistent with instrument meteorological conditions. Based on the temperature profile, the cloud droplets and precipitation were in a supercooled liquid state that put the airplane at risk of structural icing. However, the airplane was equipped with deicing boots, and the performance study data showed no increase in the airplane's drag, which was indicative of ice accumulation, before the airplane's departure from straight flight.
The airplane sustained structural damage during at least one of the airspeed exceedances and eventually broke apart in flight. The wing spar box signatures and fuselage witness marks from contact with the wing leading edge de-ice boots suggested positive wing loading before the in-flight breakup. The left horizontal stabilizer, vertical stabilizer, rudder, elevator, right aileron, right flap, and the outboard portion of the right wing were not located at the accident site and likely separated as a result of the in-flight breakup.
The pilot would not have had out-of-cockpit visual reference for the majority of the end of flight. The investigation considered the possibility that the pilot experienced spatial disorientation after taking control of the airplane from the autopilot during the descent. Although the tightening turn is consistent with a loss of control due to spatial disorientation, the pilot had over 1,300 hours of actual instrument flight experience and likely would have been aware of the possibility of such illusory effects. Additionally, the lowest cloud bases were about 10,000 ft which would have given the pilot a small amount of time to regain orientation if he had become disoriented. It is possible that the airplane's deviation from the intended track (indicative of the airplane no longer under autopilot control), whether pilot induced or not, was the result of a structural failure.

Analysis of weather sounding data also indicated strong vertical wind shear between 13,000 ft and 16,000 ft and a high possibility of moderate or greater turbulence within those altitudes. Accordingly, the investigation also considered the possibility that the airspeed exceedances during the descent, combined with the moderate and greater turbulence forecast for the area just below the airplane's flight path, resulted in structural damage to the airplane that rendered it uncontrollable. Given that the loss of control happened within about 20 seconds from the time the airplane deviated from its flight path (no longer under autopilot control) and that the pilot (who was experienced in actual instrument conditions) was not able to recover airplane control, the airplane likely sustained airframe damage from the airspeed exceedances during the descent that prevented the pilot or autopilot from maintaining control.
A medical review revealed the pilot's coronary artery disease was associated with some increased risk of an impairing or incapacitating cardiovascular event such as chest pain, abnormal heartbeat, or heart attack. Although such an event does not leave reliable autopsy evidence if it occurs immediately before death, there is no autopsy evidence that such an event occurred. Additionally, the pilot's postmortem toxicology results indicate that he had used phentermine. The phentermine results in postmortem urine and tissue provided no clear evidence that the pilot was experiencing significant associated impairing effects at the time of the accident.
Probable Cause: The pilot's exceedance of the airplane's design limitations, which resulted in an in-flight breakup.

SAN DIEGO -- The U.S. Marine Corps says the pilot of an F-35B stealth fighter is expected to live after ejecting from the jet before it crashed in California.
The jet went down Friday near the Miramar air base in San Diego. “The pilot ejected, was transported to a local medical facility in stable condition for evaluation and treatment of non-life-threatening injuries,” the Marine Corps said in an updated statement.
Aerial video from a news helicopter showed a plume of black smoke rising from the wreckage in a dirt field, with multiple military and firefighting vehicles and people standing nearby. What appeared to be white flame retardant covered the ground, and at least one person was spraying the wreckage with a fire hose.
Wade Lott saw the crash as he drove to work at a concrete company just south of the flight line.
“It just blew up, it was crazy,” said Lott, 36, who watched from his truck as two jets descended toward the runway together. The first landed without incident, but the second suddenly began slowing down, almost as if it were trying to hover, Lott said. When the jet was about 100 feet (30 m) above the ground, the pilot ejected and their parachute deployed as they rose about 200 feet (61 m) into the air just in time.
“The jet hit the ground right next to another plane,” said Lott. “It plowed into the runway and just blew up.”
Candace Hadley, a spokesperson for San Diego Fire, said firefighters were on scene to respond to a vegetation fire that sparked near the crash site. She referred additional questions to Marine Corps Air Station Miramar.
The base used to host the Navy fighter pilot training school depicted in the original “Top Gun” movie, and was known as “Fightertown USA” in its heyday. The school was relocated to Naval Air Station Fallon in Nevada in 1996 after the base was transferred to the Marine Corps.
texts.1: The U.S. Marine Corps, Navy and Air Force together have more than 630 F-35s, according to a 2024 analysis by the Government Accounting Office, which estimated the overall price tag to be $2 trillion at that point. The F-35B is one of several versions, and has an engine designed for short takeoffs and vertical landings. A single F-35B costs about $109 million.
texts.2:
## Top Stories
A Marines statement called Friday’s crash a “Class A mishap.” That’s the most severe mishap category, used when the damage totals more than $2 million, an aircraft is destroyed or a service member killed. In the Air Force alone, there have been at least 17 other “Class A mishaps” involving F-35 aircraft since 2000, according to Air Force Safety Center statistics.
At least seven other military aircraft mishaps have happened in the U.S. this year, according to the Flight Safety Foundation’s Aviation Safety Network database.
The F-35s are considered the safest and most capable fighter jets the military has in its fleet, according to the Lexington Institute think tank that focuses on defense technology and national security.
There have been fewer crashes involving any of the F-35 models since the jet was adopted in 2015 compared to other fighters when those planes were new, and fatal crashes are rare in F-35s.
In five F-35 crashes, the pilots were able to eject, though at least one sustained injuries. That pilot was injured when an F-35 crashed near the international airport in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in May 2024. The jet was heading an Air Force base in California from Texas.

Date:Sunday 12 May 2024  
Time:19:56  
Type:
Piper PA-46-500TP Malibu Meridian  
Owner/operator:Bryants Aviation Inc  
Registration:N241PM  
MSN:4697150  
Year of manufacture:2003  
Fatalities:Fatalities: 2 / Occupants: 2  
Other fatalities:0  
Aircraft damage:Destroyed  
Category:Accident  
Location:near Marianna, AR - United States of America  
Phase:En route  
Nature:Private  
Departure airport:Pensacola Regional Airport, FL (PNS/KPNS)  
Destination airport:Batesville Regional Airport, AR (BVX/KBVX)  
Investigating agency:NTSB  
Confidence Rating: Accident investigation report completed and information captured
Narrative:
On May 12, 2024, about 1956 central daylight time, a Piper PA46-500TP airplane, N241PM, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Marianna, Arkansas. The pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.   
The pilot departed about 1721 central daylight time (all times CDT unless otherwise noted) on an instrument flight rules cross-country flight with one passenger and two dogs. After departure, the airplane turned onto a northwesterly track toward the destination. The pilot requested flight level (FL) 280 and, at 1841, reported to air traffic control (ATC) that his satellite weather radar was not functioning; he later asked for assistance navigating through weather. At 1908, he reported light chop over the previous 40 miles but that the flight was currently smooth.
texts.1:
At 1944, ATC instructed the pilot to descend to FL 240 and the pilot then checked in with a new ATC center on his route and reported descending with moderate chop. ATC responded by instructing the pilot to descend at his discretion to 17,000 ft msl (all altitudes in msl unless otherwise noted). The airplane reached FL 240 (the previously instructed altitude) at 1949, where it stayed for less than a minute before continuing its descent. The first portion of this descent was at a rate of 2,000 ft/min before slowing to about 1,000 ft/min.
At 1954, while the airplane was descending through 20,000 ft, ATC instructed the pilot to descend at his discretion to 6,000 ft. The airplane's rate of descent increased to more than 3,000 ft/min, and the airspeed markedly increased from 170 kts to over 200 kts, exceeding the airplane's maximum operation limit of 187 kts calibrated airspeed; the airplane was at risk of structural damage when exceeding this limitation.
Data showed that the airplane's descent then arrested about 18,000 ft (which ADS-B data recorded as the selected altitude) and it began a small climb as the airplane's airspeed began to slow below 170 kts. At the same time, the airplane began a slight right turn off of its original course that was consistent with the airplane no longer under autopilot control. Twenty seconds later, the airplane began to rapidly descend in a tightening right turn while the calibrated airspeed rapidly increased, again surpassing the maximum operation limit. ATC simultaneously lost communication and radar contact with the airplane at 7,800 ft msl. The controller attempted to contact the pilot with no response. ATC then issued an alert notification (ALNOT) and a search began.
texts.2:
Weather radar imagery showed the airplane encountering light intensity echoes as it descended from 24,000 ft consistent with instrument meteorological conditions. Based on the temperature profile, the cloud droplets and precipitation were in a supercooled liquid state that put the airplane at risk of structural icing. However, the airplane was equipped with deicing boots, and the performance study data showed no increase in the airplane's drag, which was indicative of ice accumulation, before the airplane's departure from straight flight.
The airplane sustained structural damage during at least one of the airspeed exceedances and eventually broke apart in flight. The wing spar box signatures and fuselage witness marks from contact with the wing leading edge de-ice boots suggested positive wing loading before the in-flight breakup. The left horizontal stabilizer, vertical stabilizer, rudder, elevator, right aileron, right flap, and the outboard portion of the right wing were not located at the accident site and likely separated as a result of the in-flight breakup.
The pilot would not have had out-of-cockpit visual reference for the majority of the end of flight. The investigation considered the possibility that the pilot experienced spatial disorientation after taking control of the airplane from the autopilot during the descent. Although the tightening turn is consistent with a loss of control due to spatial disorientation, the pilot had over 1,300 hours of actual instrument flight experience and likely would have been aware of the possibility of such illusory effects. Additionally, the lowest cloud bases were about 10,000 ft which would have given the pilot a small amount of time to regain orientation if he had become disoriented. It is possible that the airplane's deviation from the intended track (indicative of the airplane no longer under autopilot control), whether pilot induced or not, was the result of a structural failure.
texts.3:
Analysis of weather sounding data also indicated strong vertical wind shear between 13,000 ft and 16,000 ft and a high possibility of moderate or greater turbulence within those altitudes. Accordingly, the investigation also considered the possibility that the airspeed exceedances during the descent, combined with the moderate and greater turbulence forecast for the area just below the airplane's flight path, resulted in structural damage to the airplane that rendered it uncontrollable. Given that the loss of control happened within about 20 seconds from the time the airplane deviated from its flight path (no longer under autopilot control) and that the pilot (who was experienced in actual instrument conditions) was not able to recover airplane control, the airplane likely sustained airframe damage from the airspeed exceedances during the descent that prevented the pilot or autopilot from maintaining control.
A medical review revealed the pilot's coronary artery disease was associated with some increased risk of an impairing or incapacitating cardiovascular event such as chest pain, abnormal heartbeat, or heart attack. Although such an event does not leave reliable autopsy evidence if it occurs immediately before death, there is no autopsy evidence that such an event occurred. Additionally, the pilot's postmortem toxicology results indicate that he had used phentermine. The phentermine results in postmortem urine and tissue provided no clear evidence that the pilot was experiencing significant associated impairing effects at the time of the accident.
Probable Cause: The pilot's exceedance of the airplane's design limitations, which resulted in an in-flight breakup.

In the Air Force alone, there have been at least 17 other “Class A mishaps” involving F-35 aircraft since 2000, according to Air Force Safety Center statistics.
At least seven other military aircraft mishaps have happened in the U.S. this year, according to the Flight Safety Foundation’s Aviation Safety Network database.
The F-35s are considered the safest and most capable fighter jets the military has in its fleet, according to the Lexington Institute think tank that focuses on defense technology and national security.
There have been fewer crashes involving any of the F-35 models since the jet was adopted in 2015 compared to other fighters when those planes were new, and fatal crashes are rare in F-35s.
In five F-35 crashes, the pilots were able to eject, though at least one sustained injuries. That pilot was injured when an F-35 crashed near the international airport in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in May 2024. The jet was heading an Air Force base in California from Texas.
___
_AP Transportation Writer Josh Funk contributed to this report from Omaha, Nebraska. Rebecca Boone contributed from Boise, Idaho._

Narrative:
On May 12, 2024, about 1956 central daylight time, a Piper PA46-500TP airplane, N241PM, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Marianna, Arkansas. The pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.   
The pilot departed about 1721 central daylight time (all times CDT unless otherwise noted) on an instrument flight rules cross-country flight with one passenger and two dogs. After departure, the airplane turned onto a northwesterly track toward the destination. The pilot requested flight level (FL) 280 and, at 1841, reported to air traffic control (ATC) that his satellite weather radar was not functioning; he later asked for assistance navigating through weather. At 1908, he reported light chop over the previous 40 miles but that the flight was currently smooth.

At 1944, ATC instructed the pilot to descend to FL 240 and the pilot then checked in with a new ATC center on his route and reported descending with moderate chop. ATC responded by instructing the pilot to descend at his discretion to 17,000 ft msl (all altitudes in msl unless otherwise noted). The airplane reached FL 240 (the previously instructed altitude) at 1949, where it stayed for less than a minute before continuing its descent. The first portion of this descent was at a rate of 2,000 ft/min before slowing to about 1,000 ft/min.
At 1954, while the airplane was descending through 20,000 ft, ATC instructed the pilot to descend at his discretion to 6,000 ft. The airplane's rate of descent increased to more than 3,000 ft/min, and the airspeed markedly increased from 170 kts to over 200 kts, exceeding the airplane's maximum operation limit of 187 kts calibrated airspeed; the airplane was at risk of structural damage when exceeding this limitation.
Data showed that the airplane's descent then arrested about 18,000 ft (which ADS-B data recorded as the selected altitude) and it began a small climb as the airplane's airspeed began to slow below 170 kts. At the same time, the airplane began a slight right turn off of its original course that was consistent with the airplane no longer under autopilot control. Twenty seconds later, the airplane began to rapidly descend in a tightening right turn while the calibrated airspeed rapidly increased, again surpassing the maximum operation limit. ATC simultaneously lost communication and radar contact with the airplane at 7,800 ft msl. The controller attempted to contact the pilot with no response. ATC then issued an alert notification (ALNOT) and a search began.

Weather radar imagery showed the airplane encountering light intensity echoes as it descended from 24,000 ft consistent with instrument meteorological conditions. Based on the temperature profile, the cloud droplets and precipitation were in a supercooled liquid state that put the airplane at risk of structural icing. However, the airplane was equipped with deicing boots, and the performance study data showed no increase in the airplane's drag, which was indicative of ice accumulation, before the airplane's departure from straight flight.
The airplane sustained structural damage during at least one of the airspeed exceedances and eventually broke apart in flight. The wing spar box signatures and fuselage witness marks from contact with the wing leading edge de-ice boots suggested positive wing loading before the in-flight breakup. The left horizontal stabilizer, vertical stabilizer, rudder, elevator, right aileron, right flap, and the outboard portion of the right wing were not located at the accident site and likely separated as a result of the in-flight breakup.
The pilot would not have had out-of-cockpit visual reference for the majority of the end of flight. The investigation considered the possibility that the pilot experienced spatial disorientation after taking control of the airplane from the autopilot during the descent. Although the tightening turn is consistent with a loss of control due to spatial disorientation, the pilot had over 1,300 hours of actual instrument flight experience and likely would have been aware of the possibility of such illusory effects. Additionally, the lowest cloud bases were about 10,000 ft which would have given the pilot a small amount of time to regain orientation if he had become disoriented. It is possible that the airplane's deviation from the intended track (indicative of the airplane no longer under autopilot control), whether pilot induced or not, was the result of a structural failure.

Analysis of weather sounding data also indicated strong vertical wind shear between 13,000 ft and 16,000 ft and a high possibility of moderate or greater turbulence within those altitudes. Accordingly, the investigation also considered the possibility that the airspeed exceedances during the descent, combined with the moderate and greater turbulence forecast for the area just below the airplane's flight path, resulted in structural damage to the airplane that rendered it uncontrollable. Given that the loss of control happened within about 20 seconds from the time the airplane deviated from its flight path (no longer under autopilot control) and that the pilot (who was experienced in actual instrument conditions) was not able to recover airplane control, the airplane likely sustained airframe damage from the airspeed exceedances during the descent that prevented the pilot or autopilot from maintaining control.
A medical review revealed the pilot's coronary artery disease was associated with some increased risk of an impairing or incapacitating cardiovascular event such as chest pain, abnormal heartbeat, or heart attack. Although such an event does not leave reliable autopsy evidence if it occurs immediately before death, there is no autopsy evidence that such an event occurred. Additionally, the pilot's postmortem toxicology results indicate that he had used phentermine. The phentermine results in postmortem urine and tissue provided no clear evidence that the pilot was experiencing significant associated impairing effects at the time of the accident.
Probable Cause: The pilot's exceedance of the airplane's design limitations, which resulted in an in-flight breakup.

Title: Accident Piper PA-46-500TP Malibu Meridian N241PM, Sunday 12 May 2024
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
Date:Sunday 12 May 2024  
Time:19:56  
Type:
Piper PA-46-500TP Malibu Meridian  
Owner/operator:Bryants Aviation Inc  
Registration:N241PM  
MSN:4697150  
Year of manufacture:2003  
Fatalities:Fatalities: 2 / Occupants: 2  
Other fatalities:0  
Aircraft damage:Destroyed  
Category:Accident  
Location:near Marianna, AR - United States of America  
Phase:En route  
Nature:Private  
Departure airport:Pensacola Regional Airport, FL (PNS/KPNS)  
Destination airport:Batesville Regional Airport, AR (BVX/KBVX)  
Investigating agency:NTSB  
Confidence Rating: Accident investigation report completed and information captured
Narrative:
On May 12, 2024, about 1956 central daylight time, a Piper PA46-500TP airplane, N241PM, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Marianna, Arkansas. The pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.   
The pilot departed about 1721 central daylight time (all times CDT unless otherwise noted) on an instrument flight rules cross-country flight with one passenger and two dogs. After departure, the airplane turned onto a northwesterly track toward the destination. The pilot requested flight level (FL) 280 and, at 1841, reported to air traffic control (ATC) that his satellite weather radar was not functioning; he later asked for assistance navigating through weather. At 1908, he reported light chop over the previous 40 miles but that the flight was currently smooth.

At 1944, ATC instructed the pilot to descend to FL 240 and the pilot then checked in with a new ATC center on his route and reported descending with moderate chop. ATC responded by instructing the pilot to descend at his discretion to 17,000 ft msl (all altitudes in msl unless otherwise noted). The airplane reached FL 240 (the previously instructed altitude) at 1949, where it stayed for less than a minute before continuing its descent. The first portion of this descent was at a rate of 2,000 ft/min before slowing to about 1,000 ft/min.
At 1954, while the airplane was descending through 20,000 ft, ATC instructed the pilot to descend at his discretion to 6,000 ft. The airplane's rate of descent increased to more than 3,000 ft/min, and the airspeed markedly increased from 170 kts to over 200 kts, exceeding the airplane's maximum operation limit of 187 kts calibrated airspeed; the airplane was at risk of structural damage when exceeding this limitation.
Data showed that the airplane's descent then arrested about 18,000 ft (which ADS-B data recorded as the selected altitude) and it began a small climb as the airplane's airspeed began to slow below 170 kts. At the same time, the airplane began a slight right turn off of its original course that was consistent with the airplane no longer under autopilot control. Twenty seconds later, the airplane began to rapidly descend in a tightening right turn while the calibrated airspeed rapidly increased, again surpassing the maximum operation limit. ATC simultaneously lost communication and radar contact with the airplane at 7,800 ft msl. The controller attempted to contact the pilot with no response. ATC then issued an alert notification (ALNOT) and a search began.

Weather radar imagery showed the airplane encountering light intensity echoes as it descended from 24,000 ft consistent with instrument meteorological conditions. Based on the temperature profile, the cloud droplets and precipitation were in a supercooled liquid state that put the airplane at risk of structural icing. However, the airplane was equipped with deicing boots, and the performance study data showed no increase in the airplane's drag, which was indicative of ice accumulation, before the airplane's departure from straight flight.
The airplane sustained structural damage during at least one of the airspeed exceedances and eventually broke apart in flight. The wing spar box signatures and fuselage witness marks from contact with the wing leading edge de-ice boots suggested positive wing loading before the in-flight breakup. The left horizontal stabilizer, vertical stabilizer, rudder, elevator, right aileron, right flap, and the outboard portion of the right wing were not located at the accident site and likely separated as a result of the in-flight breakup.
The pilot would not have had out-of-cockpit visual reference for the majority of the end of flight. The investigation considered the possibility that the pilot experienced spatial disorientation after taking control of the airplane from the autopilot during the descent. Although the tightening turn is consistent with a loss of control due to spatial disorientation, the pilot had over 1,300 hours of actual instrument flight experience and likely would have been aware of the possibility of such illusory effects. Additionally, the lowest cloud bases were about 10,000 ft which would have given the pilot a small amount of time to regain orientation if he had become disoriented. It is possible that the airplane's deviation from the intended track (indicative of the airplane no longer under autopilot control), whether pilot induced or not, was the result of a structural failure.

Analysis of weather sounding data also indicated strong vertical wind shear between 13,000 ft and 16,000 ft and a high possibility of moderate or greater turbulence within those altitudes. Accordingly, the investigation also considered the possibility that the airspeed exceedances during the descent, combined with the moderate and greater turbulence forecast for the area just below the airplane's flight path, resulted in structural damage to the airplane that rendered it uncontrollable. Given that the loss of control happened within about 20 seconds from the time the airplane deviated from its flight path (no longer under autopilot control) and that the pilot (who was experienced in actual instrument conditions) was not able to recover airplane control, the airplane likely sustained airframe damage from the airspeed exceedances during the descent that prevented the pilot or autopilot from maintaining control.
A medical review revealed the pilot's coronary artery disease was associated with some increased risk of an impairing or incapacitating cardiovascular event such as chest pain, abnormal heartbeat, or heart attack. Although such an event does not leave reliable autopsy evidence if it occurs immediately before death, there is no autopsy evidence that such an event occurred. Additionally, the pilot's postmortem toxicology results indicate that he had used phentermine. The phentermine results in postmortem urine and tissue provided no clear evidence that the pilot was experiencing significant associated impairing effects at the time of the accident.
Probable Cause: The pilot's exceedance of the airplane's design limitations, which resulted in an in-flight breakup.

MARIANNA, Ark. (KAIT) - The National Transportation Safety Board has released its final report on a 2024 plane crash that killed a Batesville couple.
Joseph Bryant and his wife, Sharon, died May 12, 2024, when their Piper PA46-500TP airplane crashed in a field near Marianna, Arkansas.
Joseph Bryant and his wife, Sharon, died May 12, 2024, when their Piper PA46-500TP airplane crashed in a field near Marianna, Arkansas.(National Transportation Safety Board)

# NTSB: Speed, structural failure caused deadly 2024 crash that killed Batesville couple
## The flight
The couple and their two small dogs departed Pensacola International Airport in Florida at 5:21 p.m. CDT, bound for Batesville Regional Airport.
Around 7:55 p.m., near Marianna, the plane entered a rapid descent and began spiraling, the NTSB said.
“The airplane’s speed rapidly increased from 160 kts to 290 kts,” the report said. “The airplane’s increasing speed in the descending tight turn exceeded the airplane’s structural limitations.”

# NTSB: Speed, structural failure caused deadly 2024 crash that killed Batesville couple
## The wreckage
The plane’s wreckage was found in a field around 11 p.m. Parts of the aircraft, including the wings and stabilizers, were separated from the fuselage. Some parts were never recovered, the report said.
The couple’s two small dogs were not located at the scene or within the wreckage.

# NTSB: Speed, structural failure caused deadly 2024 crash that killed Batesville couple
## Findings
An autopsy conducted at the Arkansas State Crime Laboratory determined Joseph Bryant, who was piloting the plane, died of multiple traumatic injuries and ruled the death an accident.
Postmortem toxicological testing by the FAA Forensic Sciences Laboratory found traces of phentermine, which can impair alertness. The NTSB noted that phentermine, which is used for weight loss, can cause irregular heartbeats and delirium. However, the autopsy found no evidence of a cardiac event.
The NTSB noted strong vertical wind shear caused moderate turbulence, but a performance study showed no increase in the airplane’s drag before it departed from straight flight.
The report also noted that the airplane was likely flying through clouds and encountered structural icing conditions at the time of the crash.
“The presence of the echoes indicated that the airplane was in clouds or instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) and, based on the temperature profile, the cloud droplets and precipitation were in the supercooled liquid state and structural icing conditions,” the report said.
The NTSB concluded the crash resulted from the pilot exceeding the aircraft’s speed limits, which caused in-flight structural failure.

## Crash of a Beechcraft BeechJet 400A in Bentonville
During the takeoff the pilot pulled the airplane’s control yoke aft to rotate and the airplane lifted off the runway as normal. The nose of the airplane dropped, and the pilot applied additional backpressure on the yoke. The pilot reported he felt a “snap” followed by a lack of tension on the control yoke. The airplane pitched down and settled back on the runway. The pilot applied maximum braking and full thrust reverse; however, the airplane continued off the end of the runway. The pilot applied left rudder and brake to turn the airplane to avoid contacting a gas station. The landing gear collapsed during the turn, which resulted in substantial damage to the right wing when it struck the ground. Two passengers escaped with minor injuries and seven others occupants were unarmed. The airplane was damaged beyond repair. A postaccident examination of the airplane revealed the elevator control cable was fractured at a pulley bracket near the aft portion of the fuselage where the cable transitioned from a horizontal to a vertical orientation. A metallurgical examination found nearly all the wires of the cable had rubbing damage to varying extents around the sides of the wires near the fracture. The upper guard pin exhibited wear, scratch marks, and gouges. The pulley contained several isolated wire fragments. The damage on the cable, upper guard pin on the pulley, and the pulley assembly was consistent with the cable having been improperly routed on the wrong side of the upper guard pin. Over time, the cable likely rubbed against the upper guard pin until the cable was sufficiently damaged to produce failure under normal operating loads. A review of the maintenance logbook entries found that the elevator cable was replaced about a year before the accident and that the airplane flew about 316.5 hours before the cable separated.
Probable cause:
Improper rigging of the elevator cable over the upper guard pin, which resulted in a cable separation and loss of elevator control.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has released its final report into the fatal May 12, 2024 crash of a Piper PA-46-500TP Malibu Meridian near Marianna, Arkansas, providing new insight into the chain of events that led to the aircraft's in-flight breakup and the deaths of both people on board.
The turboprop aircraft, registered as N241PM, departed Pensacola, Florida, on an IFR flight to Batesville, Arkansas, with the pilot, one passenger, and two dogs aboard. During the cruise, the pilot reported that the aircraft's satellite weather radar was not functioning and later requested assistance navigating around weather. While descending from Flight Level 280, air traffic controllers advised the pilot of moderate turbulence ahead and issued progressively lower altitude clearances.

# The National Transportation Safety... - Flight RouteXplorer | Facebook
## Flight RouteXplorer's Post
As the aircraft descended through 20,000 feet, investigators found that its speed rapidly increased beyond the aircraft's maximum operating limit of 187 knots calibrated airspeed. The descent rate exceeded 3,000 feet per minute before briefly stabilizing. Moments later, the aircraft deviated from its previously stable course, suggesting it was no longer under autopilot control. Within about 20 seconds, it entered a tightening right-hand turn, accelerated even further, and disappeared from radar at approximately 7,800 feet. Air traffic controllers immediately lost radio contact and initiated search procedures.
The investigation determined that the aircraft exceeded its structural design limitations during the high-speed descent. The excessive aerodynamic loads caused catastrophic structural failure, leading to an in-flight breakup. Large portions of the aircraft, including sections of the wings and tail, separated before impact, leaving investigators to recover wreckage spread across the accident area.
Although weather analysis identified strong vertical wind shear and the likelihood of moderate turbulence, investigators found no evidence that structural icing had accumulated on the aircraft despite the presence of supercooled liquid water within clouds. The report also considered the possibility of spatial disorientation but concluded that the experienced instrument-rated pilot likely lost control because the aircraft had already sustained structural damage from exceeding its airspeed limitations.
The NTSB determined that the probable cause of the accident was the pilot's exceedance of the airplane's design limitations, which resulted in an in-flight breakup. The findings also cited the aircraft's wing spar and airspeed limitations being exceeded, along with environmental conditions that affected the operation of the flight.
This accident serves as another reminder of how quickly a combination of turbulence, high descent rates, and excessive airspeed can overwhelm even a capable aircraft. The report highlights the critical importance of remaining within certified operating limits, particularly during instrument meteorological conditions and turbulent descents, where structural margins can be be exceeded in a matter of seconds.

## Crash of a Piper PA-46-500TP Malibu Meridian in Marianna: 2 killed
The pilot departed about 1721 central daylight time (all times CDT unless otherwise noted) on an instrument flight rules cross-country flight with one passenger and two dogs. After departure, the airplane turned onto a northwesterly track toward the destination. The pilot requested flight level (FL) 280 and, at 1841, reported to air traffic control (ATC) that his satellite weather radar was not functioning; he later asked for assistance navigating through weather. At 1908, he reported light chop over the previous 40 miles but that the flight was currently smooth. At 1944, ATC instructed the pilot to descend to FL 240 and the pilot then checked in with a new ATC center on his route and reported descending with moderate chop. ATC responded by instructing the pilot to descend at his discretion to 17,000 ft msl (all altitudes in msl unless otherwise noted). The airplane reached FL 240 (the previously instructed altitude) at 1949, where it stayed for less than a minute before continuing its descent. The first portion of this descent was at a rate of 2,000 ft/min before slowing to about 1,000 ft/min. At 1954, while the airplane was descending through 20,000 ft, ATC instructed the pilot to descend at his discretion to 6,000 ft. The airplane’s rate of descent increased to more than 3,000 ft/min, and the airspeed markedly increased from 170 kts to over 200 kts, exceeding the airplane’s maximum operation limit of 187 kts calibrated airspeed; the airplane was at risk of structural damage when exceeding this limitation. Data showed that the airplane’s descent then arrested about 18,000 ft (which ADS-B data recorded as the selected altitude) and it began a small climb as the airplane’s airspeed began to slow below 170 kts. At the same time, the airplane began a slight right turn off of its original course that was consistent with the airplane no longer under autopilot control.

## Crash of a Piper PA-46-500TP Malibu Meridian in Marianna: 2 killed
Twenty seconds later, the airplane began to rapidly descend in a tightening right turn while the calibrated airspeed rapidly increased, again surpassing the maximum operation limit. ATC simultaneously lost communication and radar contact with the airplane at 7,800 ft msl. The controller attempted to contact the pilot with no response. ATC then issued an alert notification (ALNOT) and a search began. The wreckage was found near Marianna. Both occupants were killed.
Probable cause:
The pilot’s exceedance of the airplane’s design limitations, which resulted in an in-flight breakup. Analysis of weather sounding data also indicated strong vertical wind shear between 13,000 ft and 16,000 ft and a high possibility of moderate or greater turbulence within those altitudes. Accordingly, the investigation also considered the possibility that the airspeed exceedances during the descent, combined with the moderate and greater turbulence forecast for the area just below the airplane’s flight path, resulted in structural damage to the airplane that rendered it uncontrollable.

## Crash of a Beechcraft BeechJet 400A in Bentonville
During the takeoff the pilot pulled the airplane’s control yoke aft to rotate and the airplane lifted off the runway as normal. The nose of the airplane dropped, and the pilot applied additional backpressure on the yoke. The pilot reported he felt a “snap” followed by a lack of tension on the control yoke. The airplane pitched down and settled back on the runway. The pilot applied maximum braking and full thrust reverse; however, the airplane continued off the end of the runway. The pilot applied left rudder and brake to turn the airplane to avoid contacting a gas station. The landing gear collapsed during the turn, which resulted in substantial damage to the right wing when it struck the ground. Two passengers escaped with minor injuries and seven others occupants were unarmed. The airplane was damaged beyond repair. A postaccident examination of the airplane revealed the elevator control cable was fractured at a pulley bracket near the aft portion of the fuselage where the cable transitioned from a horizontal to a vertical orientation. A metallurgical examination found nearly all the wires of the cable had rubbing damage to varying extents around the sides of the wires near the fracture. The upper guard pin exhibited wear, scratch marks, and gouges. The pulley contained several isolated wire fragments. The damage on the cable, upper guard pin on the pulley, and the pulley assembly was consistent with the cable having been improperly routed on the wrong side of the upper guard pin. Over time, the cable likely rubbed against the upper guard pin until the cable was sufficiently damaged to produce failure under normal operating loads. A review of the maintenance logbook entries found that the elevator cable was replaced about a year before the accident and that the airplane flew about 316.5 hours before the cable separated.
Probable cause:
Improper rigging of the elevator cable over the upper guard pin, which resulted in a cable separation and loss of elevator control.
Final Report:
